english.html: O how ill-easy it is that the crime should not manifest and discover itself in the face! And as to his now denying it: besides that this cannot alter nor change the truth of the matter <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, there is no one who does not know that to what an accused man says (even were he at the point of death) to charge another, or to discharge himself, no great faith is given <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. For neither can the assertion of one man harm another <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup> — as Moses himself had written in his laws <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup> — nor can anyone (though he be esteemed a great man of worth, and placed in honour and great authority <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>) bear witness in his own cause <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>. Although, to the profit of another, the assertion of a third party may sometimes avail: as for example, the declaration made by one who is about to die of some wound, the author of which is uncertain, tending to the discharge of another who is accused of having struck the blow, is of such force, and so profits the accused, that he cannot afterwards be put to the torture, even though otherwise the indications were sufficient <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>.

notes.gloss: Adsumptio originis quae non est, veritati non praeiudicat: claiming an origin that is not one's own does not prejudice the truth — hence the denial cannot change the truth of the matter.

notes.gloss: For the dying man's declaration that clears another of the blow, which bars the torture of the accused; C. cõ. de leg. is read as Communia de legatis; a reading as C. de legibus (C. 1.14) is possible.

english.html: For the rest, he confesses to having been a very bad scapegrace in all ways: even to having committed several thefts and acts of cheating.

This was a great conjecture, as we have represented above <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, against the said du Tilh: inasmuch as of one who has been bad and wicked in the past there is great occasion to presume that he is still such, and perseveres in like malice <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>.

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation XXXVII (annot-037, p058), on the presumption that one once wicked remains so
notes.gloss: At p058 the printed and the counted numbers still agree.

notes.citation: Liber Sextus, De regulis iuris, regula 8 (Semel malus semper praesumitur esse malus)
notes.original: c. ſemel malus. de reg. iur.
notes.gloss: Once bad, always presumed bad — the maxim of the Sext, cited without in VI; the civil-law title D. 50.17 has no such rule.
